intro: A child has her father's chin and her grandmother's laugh. A field of corn stands in rows of plants that are nearly identical. A family learns that a rare disease runs in its genes. All three are the same story. Something inside cells carries instructions. It copies them, hands them on, and once in a while changes them. This unit is about that something.

The first chapter goes inside the cell. You will see the shape of DNA and how a cell copies it. You will see how a gene becomes a protein, and how a change of one base can change a life. You will follow Gregor Mendel's peas to learn why traits skip a generation. You will follow Queen Victoria's family to watch a gene ride down an X chromosome. The chapter ends with the tools that let scientists read a whole genome and edit a single base, and the questions those tools raise.

By the end you should be able to read a DNA sequence into a protein, explain how a single changed base can matter, and use a Punnett square and a pedigree to predict how a trait will show up in a family.
bigQuestion: How do living things store, copy and pass on the instructions that make them who they are?

test.q: Which base pairs with cytosine in DNA?
test.why: The pairing rule is A with T and G with C.

test.q: The order of steps from gene to protein is:
test.why: A gene is first transcribed into mRNA, then the mRNA is translated into protein.

test.q: Deleting two bases from the middle of a gene will most likely:
choices: Shift the reading frame and change every codon after it
test.why: Two is not a multiple of three, so every codon downstream is read out of frame.

test.q: Which process creates new combinations of alleles in sex cells?
test.why: Crossing over and independent assortment during meiosis shuffle alleles into new combinations.

test.q: A cross between two Rr pea plants gives what ratio of round to wrinkled seeds?
test.why: The Punnett square gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr: three round to one wrinkled.

test.q: Red-green color blindness is much more common in men because the allele is:
choices: Recessive and on the X chromosome
test.why: Men have one X, so one recessive allele shows. Women need it on both X chromosomes.

test.q: In a pedigree, two unshaded parents have a shaded child. The trait is:
test.why: Only a recessive allele can be carried unseen by both parents and appear in a child.

test.q: What does CRISPR-Cas9 use to find its target in DNA?
choices: A guide RNA matching the target sequence
A protein that reads amino acids
test.why: The guide RNA pairs with the matching DNA sequence and directs Cas9 to cut there.

test.q: Who took Photo 51, the X-ray image that revealed DNA's helical shape?
test.why: Franklin and Gosling made Photo 51 in 1952; Watson and Crick used it to build their model.

test.q: A mutation changes one base in a gene, but the protein comes out the same. The most likely reason is:
choices: Proteins are never affected by DNA
The new codon codes for the same amino acid
test.why: Most amino acids have several codons, so some base changes are silent.

choices: Exactly the same DNA as the parent cell
Half the number of chromosomes, in new combinations
test.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and shuffles alleles, so each egg or sperm is unique.

test.q: A trait appears in a child but in neither parent. The trait is most likely:
choices: Recessive, with both parents carrying one hidden copy
test.why: Two carriers of a recessive allele can each pass it on, giving a child two copies.

test.q: Pesticide resistance in insects develops because:
choices: Rare resistant insects survive and reproduce
Insects learn to avoid the spray
Farmers breed resistant insects on purpose
test.why: Spraying selects for resistance alleles already present in a few individuals.

test.q: Two populations of a species are split by a new river for a million years. The most likely result is:
choices: They merge into one larger species
They gather different changes and may become separate species
test.why: Without gene flow, mutation, selection and drift push the two groups apart.

test.q: Which sequence describes how a gene makes a protein?
choices: Proteins are built directly from DNA
mRNA is copied into DNA and then into protein
DNA is read into mRNA, which is translated into protein
test.why: Transcription copies DNA into mRNA; translation at the ribosome reads mRNA into a protein.

write.prompt: Make a claim: should families be offered genetic testing for inherited diseases before having children? Use at least three ideas from this unit (for example how recessive alleles are carried, what a Punnett square predicts, and what a mutation does to a protein) and weigh the benefits against the concerns.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence at the start.
Use at least three science ideas from the unit, each with a specific example.
Show a Punnett square if it helps your argument.
Address the other side fairly: what is the strongest concern, and how do you answer it?
Use science words correctly: allele, recessive, carrier, genotype, phenotype.

title: Biology: Genetics and Inheritance

chapters.title: DNA, Genes and Inheritance
chapters.bigQuestion: How does a molecule inside a cell carry instructions, copy them, and pass them from parents to children?

story.title: The Picture That Showed the Shape of DNA
story.kicker: In 1952 a single X-ray photograph, taken in a basement lab in London, gave away the secret of the molecule of life.
paragraphs: Picture a thin strand of DNA pulled out of a cell, wet and stretched like a fine thread. Now imagine firing a beam of X-rays through it. The rays bounce off the atoms inside and land on a piece of film. They do not make a photo of the molecule. They make a pattern of spots and smears. If you know how to read the pattern, it tells you the shape of the thing the rays passed through.

In May 1952, at King's College in London, the chemist Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling took such a picture. They labeled it Photo 51. It showed a bold X made of dark smudges. Franklin knew what an X like that meant. It is the signature of a helix, a shape like a spiral staircase. From the spacing of the smudges she could measure the size of the steps and the width of the whole spiral.

Franklin worked slowly and carefully. She wanted the measurements right before she said what the shape was. Meanwhile, at Cambridge, James Watson and Francis Crick were building models out of metal plates and wire, trying shapes until one fit the facts. In January 1953, Franklin's colleague Maurice Wilkins showed Watson Photo 51. Franklin did not know he had done it. Watson later wrote that his pulse raced when he saw it.

Within weeks Watson and Crick had a model that fit everything: two strands winding around each other, with paired bases inside like rungs on a twisted ladder. Their short paper appeared in the journal Nature on April 25, 1953. Franklin's own paper, with the measurements from Photo 51, appeared in the same issue. But hers was printed as if it merely supported their idea, not as the evidence that made it possible.

Franklin died of cancer in 1958, at the age of 37. In 1962 the Nobel Prize went to Watson, Crick and Wilkins. The prize is never given to someone who has died, so her name was not on it. Today scientists argue about how much credit she was owed. What no one argues about is the picture. The X on Photo 51 was real, the measurements were right, and they showed the shape that every living thing uses to store its instructions.
story.think: Franklin's data were used without her knowledge. What rules should scientists follow about sharing unpublished work, and why?

lessons.title: A Twisted Ladder
lessons.mainIdea: DNA is a double helix: two backbones with paired bases inside, and the pairing rule lets it store information.
reading: Every cell that has a nucleus keeps its instructions in a molecule called *DNA*. If you could unwind the DNA from one human cell and lay it out straight, it would be about 2 meters long. Yet it fits inside a nucleus far too small to see without a microscope. It fits because it is a very thin thread, about 2 nanometers wide, coiled and folded again and again.

The shape of the thread is a *double helix*. Think of a ladder. Now twist the ladder into a spiral. The two rails of the ladder are long chains of sugar and phosphate. The rungs are made of pairs of smaller molecules called *bases*. There are only four bases: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). Each rung is one base from one rail reaching across to one base on the other.

The bases do not pair at random. A always pairs with T, and G always pairs with C. This is the *base-pairing* rule. It works because of shape and chemistry. A and T fit together with two weak hydrogen bonds. G and C fit with three. A pair of A with G would be too wide; a pair of C with T would be too narrow. The ladder only stays even when the rule is followed.

The order of the bases along one rail is the information. A stretch reading ATTGCA means something different from ATTGCC. Human DNA holds about 3 billion base pairs. Because of the pairing rule, if you know one rail you can write the other. That simple fact, as you will see, is how a cell copies its instructions.

words.d: deoxyribonucleic acid, the molecule that stores a cell's instructions
the twisted-ladder shape of DNA, with two strands winding around each other
one of four small molecules (A, T, G, C) whose order along DNA spells the instructions
the rule that A always pairs with T and G always pairs with C

look.title: What Photo 51 Measured
look.cite: standard reference values from X-ray studies of DNA, 1950s
look.prompt: How many base pairs fit in one full turn of the helix? Show how the numbers tell you.

check.q: One strand of DNA reads GATTC. What does the matching strand read?
check.why: G pairs with C, A with T, T with A. So GATTC pairs with CTAAG.

check.q: Why can A not pair with G?
choices: They are both found only in RNA
The pair would be too wide to fit between the rails
They carry the same electric charge
G is only found in bacteria
check.why: A and G are both the larger kind of base. Two large bases together would push the rails apart.

check.q: Where is the information in DNA stored?
choices: In the sugar and phosphate rails
In the twist of the helix
In the order of the bases
In the number of hydrogen bonds
check.why: The rails are the same everywhere. What changes from gene to gene is the sequence of bases.

lessons.title: Copying the Code
lessons.mainIdea: Before a cell divides, it unzips its DNA and builds a new partner strand for each half, following the pairing rule.
reading: A cell in your skin divides. Each of the two new cells needs a complete set of DNA. That means the whole 3 billion base pairs must be copied first, with almost no mistakes. The double helix makes this possible. Because each strand is the mirror of the other, each strand can serve as a template, or pattern, for building a new one.

*Replication* starts when an enzyme called helicase unzips the helix. It breaks the weak hydrogen bonds between the base pairs and pulls the two strands apart. Now each old strand has its bases exposed. A second enzyme, *DNA polymerase*, moves along each old strand. It grabs free bases floating in the cell and snaps them into place, always following the rule: A across from T, G across from C.

When it is done, there are two double helices where there was one. Each contains one old strand and one new strand. Scientists call this *semiconservative* copying, because half of each new molecule is conserved from the original. In 1958 Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl proved it by growing bacteria in food with heavy nitrogen, then switching to light nitrogen and weighing the DNA after each round of division.

DNA polymerase also checks its work. If it places a wrong base, it usually backs up and fixes it. Even so, a few errors slip through, roughly one for every billion bases copied. Those rare errors are called *mutations*, and later in this chapter you will see that they are the raw material of change.

words.d: the process of copying DNA before a cell divides
the enzyme that builds a new DNA strand by matching bases to a template strand
describes copying in which each new DNA molecule keeps one old strand and gets one new strand
a change in the sequence of bases in DNA

look.title: A Sentence at the End of a Short Paper
look.text: Near the end of their 1953 paper, Watson and Crick noted, almost in passing, that the specific base pairing they proposed immediately suggested a way for the genetic material to be copied.
look.prompt: Why does the pairing rule 'suggest' a way of copying? Explain the idea in your own words.

check.q: After one round of replication, what does each new DNA molecule contain?
choices: One old strand and one new strand
check.why: Each old strand serves as a template. The result is one old plus one new strand, which is semiconservative.

check.q: What does helicase do?
check.why: Helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds and unzips the double helix so each strand can be copied.

check.q: If DNA polymerase lost its ability to check its work, what would you expect?
choices: More mutations in the new DNA
The helix would unwind by itself
Faster cell growth with no side effects
check.why: Proofreading catches most wrong bases. Without it, more errors would remain in the copy.

lessons.title: Writing the Message
lessons.mainIdea: A gene is copied into a strand of messenger RNA that can leave the nucleus and carry the instructions to the cell's protein-building machines.
reading: DNA stays in the nucleus, but the work of the cell happens outside it. Proteins do that work: they build structures, speed up reactions and carry signals. So the cell needs a way to send the instructions for a protein out of the nucleus without sending the DNA itself. It does this with a messenger.

A *gene* is a stretch of DNA that holds the instructions for one protein. To read it, an enzyme called RNA polymerase unzips just that stretch and builds a single strand of *RNA* alongside it. RNA is a close cousin of DNA. It has one strand, not two, and it uses a base called uracil (U) in place of thymine (T). So where DNA reads ATG, the RNA copy reads UAC. This copying step is called *transcription*, the way a clerk transcribes a document.

In cells with a nucleus, the first RNA copy is edited before it leaves. Some stretches, called introns, are cut out. The remaining pieces are joined. The finished strand, called *messenger RNA* or mRNA, slips through a pore in the nuclear membrane into the cytoplasm. There it is picked up by a ribosome, the machine that will turn its message into a protein.

Not every gene is transcribed all the time. A cell in your eye and a cell in your liver have the same DNA, but each turns on a different set of genes. That control is what makes the two cells different. A gene that is never read is like a recipe in a closed book: present, but not in use.

words.d: a stretch of DNA that carries the instructions for one protein
a single-stranded molecule like DNA that uses uracil in place of thymine
copying a gene from DNA into a strand of RNA
the edited RNA copy of a gene that carries its message to a ribosome

look.title: Same Book, Different Pages
look.text: A muscle cell and a nerve cell in the same person carry exactly the same DNA. Yet the muscle cell is packed with proteins that contract, and the nerve cell is packed with proteins that pass electrical signals. Neither has lost any genes.
look.prompt: If both cells have the same instructions, what must be different between them? Where in the gene-to-protein path does that difference show up?

check.q: A DNA strand reads TACGGA. What does its RNA transcript read?
check.why: RNA pairs A with U, T with A, G with C, C with G. TACGGA becomes AUGCCU.

check.q: Why does the cell make mRNA instead of sending DNA out of the nucleus?
choices: mRNA holds more information than DNA
DNA would dissolve in the cytoplasm
Ribosomes cannot read any molecule with thymine
DNA cannot fit through the membrane and is safer staying put
check.why: The DNA stays protected in the nucleus. A short, disposable RNA copy carries just the gene that is needed.

check.q: What is removed from RNA before it leaves the nucleus?
check.why: Introns are stretches cut out of the first RNA copy. The remaining pieces are joined to form mRNA.

lessons.title: Reading the Message
lessons.mainIdea: A ribosome reads mRNA three bases at a time, and each three-base codon tells it which amino acid to add to a growing protein.
reading: The mRNA has reached a ribosome. Now the message must be turned into a protein. A protein is a chain of smaller units called *amino acids*. There are 20 kinds. The order of amino acids in the chain decides how it folds, and the fold decides what it can do. The job of *translation* is to read the bases of the mRNA and string the right amino acids together in the right order.

The ribosome reads the mRNA in groups of three bases. Each group is a *codon*. With four bases there are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 possible codons, more than enough to name 20 amino acids. Most amino acids have several codons. One codon, AUG, means 'start' and also stands for the amino acid methionine. Three codons, UAA, UAG and UGA, mean 'stop'. This code is nearly the same in bacteria, oak trees and people, which is why scientists can put a human gene into bacteria and have them make a human protein, such as insulin.

Small molecules called transfer RNA, or tRNA, do the matching. Each tRNA has three bases that fit one codon on one end and carries the matching amino acid on the other. As the ribosome slides along the mRNA, the right tRNA docks at each codon and hands over its amino acid. The chain grows one unit at a time until a stop codon arrives. Then the finished protein is released to fold up and get to work.

The whole route, DNA to RNA to protein, is sometimes called the central dogma of biology. The word dogma is a bit strong, because scientists have found exceptions. Some viruses copy RNA back into DNA. But for the genes in your own cells, the path runs one way, and every protein in your body was built this way.

words.d: one of 20 building blocks that link in a chain to form a protein
building a protein by reading the codons of an mRNA
a group of three bases in mRNA that stands for one amino acid or a stop signal

look.title: The Genetic Code by the Numbers
look.prompt: There are 64 codons but only 20 amino acids. What does that tell you about how many codons some amino acids must have?

check.q: An mRNA has 300 bases between the start and stop codons. About how many amino acids will its protein have?
check.why: Each codon is three bases and codes one amino acid. 300 ÷ 3 = 100.

check.q: What does a tRNA molecule do?
choices: Carries an amino acid to the codon that matches it
check.why: Each tRNA matches one codon and delivers one specific amino acid to the ribosome.

check.q: Which codon tells the ribosome where to start?
check.why: AUG means start and codes for methionine; UAA, UAG and UGA mean stop.

lessons.title: When the Code Changes
lessons.mainIdea: A mutation changes the sequence of bases; its effect can be nothing, a small change, or a broken protein, depending on where and how it happens.
reading: In the 1940s doctors studying sickle cell disease found that the red blood cells of patients bend into a curved shape when oxygen is low. The bent cells jam in small blood vessels and cause pain. In 1949 Linus Pauling's team showed that the hemoglobin protein itself was different. Years later the cause was traced to a single base. In one gene, an A had been swapped for a T. That changed one codon, which changed one amino acid, which changed the shape of the whole protein.

A *substitution* like that swaps one base for another. Some substitutions are silent: the new codon names the same amino acid, so the protein is unchanged. Others change one amino acid, as in sickle cell. Still others create a stop codon in the middle of a gene, cutting the protein short. An *insertion* or *deletion* adds or removes bases. If the number is not a multiple of three, every codon after it is read wrong. This is a *frameshift*, and it usually wrecks the protein.

Where do mutations come from? Some are copying errors that slip past proofreading. Others are caused by damage: ultraviolet light from the sun, certain chemicals in tobacco smoke, or radiation. The cell repairs most damage, but not all. Most mutations land in stretches of DNA that do not code for anything and have no effect. A few are harmful. Rarely, one is helpful.

Which cells the mutation is in matters. A mutation in a skin cell affects only that cell and its descendants in your body. A mutation in a sperm or egg cell can be passed to a child and to every cell in that child. Only those inherited mutations can be passed down through a family.

words.d: a mutation that swaps one base for another
a mutation that adds one or more bases to a DNA sequence
a mutation that removes one or more bases from a DNA sequence
a mutation that shifts how codons are read, changing every amino acid after it

look.title: One Letter in a Sentence
look.text: Read this sentence three letters at a time: THE BIG CAT ATE THE RAT. Now delete the first T: HEB IGC ATA TET HER AT. Now instead swap the B for an F: THE FIG CAT ATE THE RAT.
look.prompt: Which change is a frameshift, and which is a substitution? Which one did more damage to the meaning, and why?

check.q: Why can a substitution sometimes have no effect on a protein?
choices: The new codon may name the same amino acid
The cell always deletes substituted bases
Proteins do not depend on amino acid order
check.why: Most amino acids have several codons. A change that keeps the same amino acid is silent.

check.q: Which mutation is most likely to change every amino acid after it?
choices: Swapping an A for a G
check.why: Removing one base shifts the reading frame. Removing three keeps the frame and loses one amino acid.

check.q: A mutation in a cell of your arm caused by sunlight will:
choices: Change your DNA in every cell
Affect only that cell and its descendants
check.why: Only mutations in sperm or egg cells are passed on. A skin-cell mutation stays in that cell line.

lessons.title: Shuffling the Deck
lessons.mainIdea: Meiosis makes sex cells with half the usual chromosomes, and crossing over and independent assortment mix the genes so every cell is different.
reading: Your DNA is packed into 46 *chromosomes*, in 23 pairs. One of each pair came from your mother, the other from your father. A sperm or egg carries only 23, one from each pair. When they join, the count returns to 46. The special kind of cell division that halves the count is called *meiosis*.

Meiosis begins like ordinary division: the DNA is copied. Then the cell divides twice. In the first division, the paired chromosomes line up side by side and are pulled to opposite ends. In the second, the copies separate. One cell becomes four, each with a single set of 23. Because it happens only in sex cells, meiosis is the bridge between generations.

Two things during meiosis make offspring different from each other. First, while paired chromosomes lie side by side, they swap pieces. This is *crossing over*. A chromosome that was purely your father's comes out with stretches from your mother's copy. Second, when the pairs line up, which member goes left and which goes right is random for each pair. This is *independent assortment*. With 23 pairs there are 2 to the 23rd power, more than 8 million, possible combinations from one parent alone.

Add crossing over, and then the random meeting of one sperm and one egg, and the number of possible children from two parents is beyond counting. Brothers and sisters share parents but not the same shuffle. Identical twins are the exception: they come from one fertilized egg that split, so they carry the same combination.

words.d: a long, coiled molecule of DNA that carries many genes
the two-step cell division that makes sex cells with half the usual number of chromosomes
the swapping of pieces between paired chromosomes during meiosis
the random way each pair of chromosomes separates, independent of the other pairs

look.title: Chromosome Counts
look.prompt: Does a higher chromosome count mean a more complex organism? What does the table say?

check.q: A human egg cell carries how many chromosomes?
check.why: Meiosis halves the number. Egg and sperm each carry 23, and together make 46.

check.q: What does crossing over do?
check.why: Paired chromosomes exchange segments, so each ends up with a mix of both parents' versions.

check.q: Why are two siblings (not identical twins) genetically different?
choices: Meiosis shuffles chromosomes differently each time
Each child gets only the father's DNA
Mutation changes all genes each generation
check.why: Crossing over and independent assortment give every sperm and egg a different mix.

lessons.title: Mendel's Peas
lessons.mainIdea: Gregor Mendel showed that traits are carried by paired factors, one from each parent, and that some versions hide others.
reading: In a monastery garden in what is now the Czech Republic, a monk named Gregor Mendel spent eight years crossing pea plants. He chose peas because they have clear traits, like round or wrinkled seeds and tall or short stems, and because he could control which plant pollinated which. Between 1856 and 1863 he grew and counted thousands of plants. He published his results in 1866. Almost no one noticed until 1900.

Here is what he found. Cross a plant with round seeds and a plant with wrinkled seeds, and every offspring has round seeds. The wrinkled *trait* seems to vanish. But let those offspring pollinate themselves, and wrinkled seeds come back in about one plant in four. Mendel counted 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled, close to a 3:1 ratio. He got the same ratio for six other traits.

Mendel explained it with factors that we now call *alleles*, versions of a gene. Each plant carries two alleles for seed shape, one from each parent. The round allele is *dominant*: if a plant has even one, its seeds are round. The wrinkled allele is *recessive*: seeds are wrinkled only when both alleles are wrinkled. When a plant makes pollen or eggs, the two alleles separate, and each sex cell gets one. This matches what you learned about meiosis, though Mendel never saw a chromosome.

A Punnett square shows the possibilities. Write one parent's alleles across the top, the other's down the side, and fill in the boxes. For two parents that each carry one round allele (R) and one wrinkled allele (r), the boxes are RR, Rr, Rr and rr. Three of four have at least one R and are round. One is rr and is wrinkled. The 3:1 ratio falls out of the square.

words.d: a feature of an organism, like seed shape or eye color
one version of a gene; each organism carries two alleles for each gene
an allele whose trait shows even when only one copy is present
an allele whose trait shows only when both copies are present

look.title: Mendel's Counts in the Second Generation
look.cite: Gregor Mendel, Experiments on Plant Hybrids, 1866
look.prompt: Divide each dominant count by its recessive count. What number keeps showing up, and why is it not exactly 3?

check.q: Two pea plants with the alleles Rr are crossed. What fraction of offspring will have wrinkled seeds?
check.why: The Punnett square gives RR, Rr, Rr, rr. Only rr is wrinkled: one in four.

check.q: A plant has round seeds. Which allele pairs could it have?
check.why: Round is dominant, so one R is enough. Both RR and Rr give round seeds.

check.q: Why did the wrinkled trait 'disappear' in the first generation and return in the second?
choices: The wrinkled allele was hidden by the dominant allele, not lost
Wrinkled seeds need a cold winter
Mendel counted wrong the first time
check.why: Every first-generation plant was Rr. The r was still there and reappeared as rr in the next generation.

lessons.title: Beyond Simple Dominance
lessons.mainIdea: Many traits do not follow a simple dominant-recessive pattern: alleles can blend, both can show, or a gene can ride on the X chromosome.
reading: Cross a red snapdragon with a white one and the offspring are pink. Neither allele hides the other. This is *incomplete dominance*. One red allele makes half as much red pigment as two, so the flower is a lighter color. Cross two pink plants, and you get red, pink and white in a 1:2:1 ratio, which shows the alleles never blended. They just shared the work.

Sometimes both alleles show fully at once. Human blood type is the classic case. The gene for the ABO blood group has three alleles. The A allele and the B allele each put a different marker on red blood cells. A person with one of each has both markers and is type AB. This is *codominance*. The third allele, O, puts no marker and is recessive to both. So type O people carry two O alleles.

Some genes sit on the X chromosome. Women have two X chromosomes; men have one X and one Y. A recessive allele on the X is usually masked in a woman by her other X. A man has no second X, so if his one X carries it, the trait shows. These are *sex-linked* traits. Red-green color blindness works this way. It affects about 1 in 12 men but only about 1 in 200 women. A colorblind man's sons never inherit it from him, because sons get his Y; his daughters get his X and become carriers.

Most human traits are more tangled still. Height, skin color and the risk of many diseases depend on many genes at once, plus food, sunlight and other conditions. That is why children are not simple averages of their parents and why a Punnett square cannot predict how tall you will be.

words.d: a pattern in which offspring with two different alleles show a blend of both traits
a pattern in which both alleles show fully at the same time
describes a gene carried on the X or Y chromosome

look.title: A Mother Who Sees Every Color
look.text: A boy is red-green colorblind. His mother can tell red from green with no trouble. So can his father. His maternal grandfather, though, has always mixed up red and green traffic lights.
look.prompt: Trace the allele. Which chromosome carried it, who passed it to whom, and why does the mother see colors normally?

check.q: Two pink snapdragons are crossed. What ratio of colors do you expect in the offspring?
check.why: Each pink plant is RW. The square gives RR (red), RW, RW (pink) and WW (white).

check.q: A person is blood type AB. What does that show about the A and B alleles?
choices: The person also has an O allele
check.why: Type AB cells carry both markers. Neither allele hides the other, which is codominance.

check.q: Why is red-green color blindness far more common in men than in women?
choices: The allele is on the Y chromosome
Men have more genes for vision
Men have only one X, so a single recessive allele shows
check.why: A woman needs the allele on both X chromosomes. A man needs it on his only X.

lessons.title: Reading a Family Tree
lessons.mainIdea: A pedigree charts a trait across generations, and its pattern reveals whether an allele is dominant, recessive or sex-linked.
reading: Geneticists cannot cross people the way Mendel crossed peas. Instead they draw a *pedigree*: a family tree that marks who has a trait. Squares stand for males and circles for females. A horizontal line joins parents; a vertical line leads down to their children. A shaded shape means the person shows the trait. Half-shading or a dot can mark a *carrier*, someone who has one copy of a recessive allele but does not show it.

The pattern tells the story. If two unaffected parents have an affected child, the trait must be recessive: both parents were carriers. If a trait appears in every generation and every affected child has an affected parent, it is likely dominant. If it shows up mostly in males and skips generations through unaffected mothers, it is probably recessive and on the X chromosome.

The most famous pedigree in history is Queen Victoria's. She carried an allele for hemophilia, a disease in which blood does not clot properly, on one of her X chromosomes. She had no symptoms. But one of her sons had the disease, and two of her daughters were carriers. Through royal marriages the allele reached the ruling families of Spain, Germany and Russia. The pattern, affected sons and carrier daughters, is exactly what a sex-linked recessive trait produces.

Pedigrees have practical uses today. A genetic counselor can use one, along with a DNA test, to tell a couple the odds that a child will inherit a condition that runs in the family. The chart cannot say what will happen to one particular child. It can only say what fraction of many such children would be expected to inherit it.

words.d: a chart that tracks a trait through the generations of a family
a person who has one copy of a recessive allele and does not show the trait
an inherited condition in which blood does not clot properly

look.title: Three Generations
look.text: A grandfather has a rare trait. None of his four children have it. Two of his grandsons, born to two different daughters, have it. No granddaughter does.
look.prompt: Is this trait most likely dominant, recessive on a regular chromosome, or recessive on the X chromosome? Give two clues from the pattern.

check.q: Two parents without a trait have a child with it. What must be true?
choices: Both parents carry a recessive allele
The child had a new mutation for certain
The trait is on the Y chromosome
check.why: An unseen trait appearing in a child is the mark of a recessive allele carried by both parents.

check.q: In a pedigree, what does a shaded circle mean?
check.why: Circles are female; shading means the person shows the trait.

check.q: Queen Victoria had no hemophilia but passed it to a son. Why?
choices: She had two affected X chromosomes
The allele was on her Y chromosome
She carried the recessive allele on one X, masked by her other X
Hemophilia skips every other generation by rule
check.why: As a carrier she had one normal X. Her son received the affected X and had no second X to mask it.

lessons.title: Sequencing a Genome
lessons.mainIdea: Scientists can now read the full order of bases in an organism's DNA, and doing so for humans changed medicine and how we see ourselves.
reading: A *genome* is the complete set of DNA in one organism. In 1990 a large team of scientists in the United States and other countries set out to read all 3 billion base pairs of the human genome. This was the Human Genome Project. It took 13 years and about 3 billion dollars, and it finished in April 2003. Today a person's genome can be *sequenced* in a day or two for a few hundred dollars.

The results held surprises. Scientists had guessed humans would have around 100,000 genes. The count came in at only about 20,000 protein-coding genes, similar to a mouse and fewer than some plants. Only about 1 to 2 percent of the genome codes for protein. Much of the rest controls when and where genes are turned on. And any two people are about 99.9 percent identical in their DNA. All human variety fits in the other 0.1 percent.

Reading genomes changed medicine. Doctors can test for the alleles behind cystic fibrosis, sickle cell disease and many cancers. Some drugs are now matched to a patient's genes. Genome tests can also confirm family relationships and help identify the cause of rare inherited diseases.

Reading your own code raises questions. Who should see it? Could an employer or an insurer use it against you? In the United States a 2008 federal law bars health insurers and most employers from using genetic information to discriminate. But privacy of DNA stored in company databases remains an open issue.

words.d: the complete set of DNA in an organism
to read the exact order of bases in a stretch of DNA
the international effort, finished in 2003, that read the full human DNA sequence

look.title: What the Project Found
look.text: The National Human Genome Research Institute reports that the Human Genome Project was declared complete in April 2003, that it produced a reference sequence of the roughly 3 billion base pairs of human DNA, and that the number of human genes turned out to be far smaller than many scientists had expected.
look.cite: National Human Genome Research Institute, NIH (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Why might scientists have expected many more genes than they found? What does the smaller number suggest about how genes are used?

check.q: About what fraction of the human genome codes for proteins?
check.why: Only a small fraction is protein-coding. Much of the rest regulates genes or has no known function.

check.q: Two unrelated people compare their genomes. How alike are they?
check.why: Human genomes differ by roughly one base in a thousand.

check.q: Which is a use of genome sequencing in medicine?
choices: Curing every disease by reading DNA
Testing for alleles linked to inherited disease
check.why: Sequencing reveals which alleles a person carries, which helps diagnose and sometimes guide treatment.

lessons.title: Editing With CRISPR
lessons.mainIdea: CRISPR lets scientists cut DNA at a chosen spot and change it, which brings real cures and hard questions about how far to go.
reading: Bacteria get infected by viruses, and some bacteria keep a memory of past infections. They store short pieces of viral DNA in their own genome, in a region called *CRISPR*. When the same virus returns, the bacterium makes an RNA copy of the stored piece. That RNA guides a protein called Cas9 to the matching spot in the virus's DNA, and Cas9 cuts it. It is an immune system made of DNA.

In 2012 Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that this system could be aimed anywhere. Give Cas9 a guide RNA that matches any sequence you choose, and it will cut there. The cell then repairs the cut, and scientists can supply a new piece of DNA for it to use as a patch. This is *gene editing*. For this work the two shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.

The first cures came fast. Sickle cell disease is caused by one changed base, as you saw. In December 2023 the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved a treatment that edits a patient's own blood-forming cells and returns them to the body. Researchers are also editing crops for drought tolerance and disease resistance. Illinois, where more than 90 percent of corn acres are planted with genetically engineered varieties, is watching closely.

The hard questions come with the power. Editing a patient's blood cells changes one person. Editing an embryo would change every cell of a person not yet born, and their children too. In 2018 a scientist in China announced he had edited the genes of twin girls before birth. Scientists worldwide condemned it, and he was sent to prison. Most countries now ban editing embryos that will be carried to birth. Who decides which conditions to edit, who can afford it, and what counts as a disease rather than a difference are questions the science alone cannot answer.

words.d: a bacterial defense system that scientists adapted to cut DNA at a chosen spot
deliberately changing the sequence of DNA in a living cell
the protein in the CRISPR system that cuts DNA where a guide RNA directs it

look.title: Two Kinds of Edit
look.text: Patient A, age 20, has sickle cell disease. Doctors remove some of her blood-forming cells, edit them, and put them back. Only her body is changed. Embryo B has the same allele. A lab could edit it before implanting it, so the child and all the child's descendants would be free of the disease.
look.prompt: What is the strongest argument for each edit? What is the strongest argument against the second? Who should get to decide?

check.q: What tells Cas9 where to cut?
choices: A guide RNA that matches the target sequence
check.why: Cas9 follows a guide RNA. Change the guide, and it cuts at a different place.

check.q: Where did the CRISPR system originally come from?
choices: A defense system in bacteria against viruses
check.why: Bacteria store pieces of viral DNA and use them to guide Cas9 to cut returning viruses.

check.q: Why do many scientists treat editing an embryo differently from editing a patient's blood cells?
choices: Embryo edits are passed on to future generations who cannot consent
Only embryos have the CRISPR system
check.why: An edited embryo carries the change in every cell, including future sperm or eggs, so it is inherited.

review.q: What did the X pattern on Photo 51 reveal about DNA?
choices: That it is shaped like a helix
That it is made of protein
review.why: An X-shaped diffraction pattern is the signature of a helix. Franklin's measurements gave its size.

review.q: Which sequence of steps is correct for making a protein?
review.why: A gene is transcribed into mRNA, then translated into protein.

review.q: A cell has 46 chromosomes. After meiosis, how many does each sex cell have, and why?
choices: 23, because half the DNA is destroyed
review.why: Meiosis pulls each pair apart, so every sex cell gets one of each pair: 23.

review.q: A plant with alleles Rr is crossed with a plant with rr. What fraction of offspring show the recessive trait?
review.why: The boxes are Rr, Rr, rr, rr. Half are rr and show the recessive trait.

review.q: A single base swap turns codon GAG into GTG in the hemoglobin gene. This kind of mutation is a:
review.why: One base replaced another, with no change in length. That is a substitution.

review.q: A trait shows in every generation, and every affected child has an affected parent. It is most likely:
review.why: Dominant traits cannot hide. If a child has it, a parent had the allele and showed it.

review.q: Why did the base-pairing rule matter so much once the structure of DNA was known?
choices: It proved genes were on chromosomes
It showed all species have 46 chromosomes
It showed DNA was a protein
It explained how DNA could be copied exactly
review.why: Since each strand determines the other, separating the strands and rebuilding partners copies the molecule.

review.q: What did the Human Genome Project show about the number of human genes?
choices: The same number as a bacterium
review.why: Scientists expected around 100,000 genes and found about 20,000 protein-coding ones.
